chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Ibn Fazal, from Al-Hasan ibn Asbat, from Abdul Rahman ibn Sayyab, who said:

I said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him): 'May I be sacrificed for you, the people are saying that it is not permissible to look at the stars, and they please me. So if they harm my religion, I have no need for anything that harms my religion; and if they do not harm my religion, by Allah, I desire them and I desire to look at them.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is not as they say; they do not harm your religion.'
Then he said: 'You are looking at something of it, much of which is not grasped and little of which is not beneficial. You calculate the rising of the Moon.'

Then he said: 'Do you know how many minutes are between Jupiter and Venus?' I said, 'No, by Allah.' He said: 'Do you know how many minutes are between Venus and the Moon?' I said, 'No.' He said: 'Do you know how many minutes are between the Sun and the Spica (Al-Sunbulah)?' I said, 'No, by Allah, I have not heard from any of the astrologers ever.'

He said: 'Do you know how many minutes are between the Spica and the Preserved Tablet (Al-Lawh Al-Mahfuz)?' I said, 'No, by Allah, I did not hear it from any astrologer ever.' He said: 'What is between each one of them and its counterpart is sixty or seventy minutes.' [Abdul Rahman expressed doubt.]

Then he said: 'O Abdul Rahman, this is a calculation; if a man calculates it and it falls upon him, he will know the reed in the middle of the bush, and count what is to its right, and count what is to its left, and count what is behind it, and count what is in front of it, until not a single reed of the bush is hidden from him.'
ai.seo_question: Is studying the stars (astronomy) permissible in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (as) distinguishes between astronomy and astrology, affirming that observing the stars does not inherently harm one's faith, contrary to popular belief. He uses the vast, incalculable distances between celestial bodies—measured in 'minutes'—to illustrate the limits of human calculation and the precision of divine creation, suggesting that while the stars are signs of God's power, their full complexity remains beyond complete human mastery.
